lessonTitle: Breast and Prostate Disease: Triple Assessment, Receptor Status and PSA Testing

blocks.text: A 43-year-old woman feels a firm, painless, irregular lump in her upper outer left breast while showering. Her grandfather, 71, has just had a raised blood test for the prostate and is anxious. Both are being asked to weigh a test result that could mean cancer, or could mean nothing at all. Understanding how breast lumps are assessed and what a hormone receptor result means, and where prostate screening helps and harms, is part of every doctor's work.

blocks.markdown: The breast is a modified apocrine gland of lobules and ducts embedded in fat and fibrous stroma, responsive to oestrogen and progesterone. Most breast lumps are benign (fibroadenoma, cysts, fibrocystic change), but **breast cancer** is the commonest cancer in women, arising mostly from ductal epithelium. Risk is raised by age, female sex, early menarche and late menopause, nulliparity, obesity and alcohol, family history, and inherited mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2.

### Triple assessment of a breast lump

Every breast lump is investigated by the same three-part approach, because no single component is sufficiently reliable. **Triple assessment** consists of: (1) **clinical assessment** by history and examination of both breasts and the axillae; (2) **imaging**, with **mammography** in women generally over about 40 (and ultrasound in addition), but **ultrasound** as the main modality in younger women whose dense breast tissue limits mammography; and (3) **tissue sampling** by **core needle biopsy** for histology, which gives both diagnosis and receptor status (fine needle aspiration for cytology is used less often). The results are concordant or discordant, and a discordant result requires further evaluation.

rows: History, examination of breasts and axillary nodes
Suspicious features: hard, irregular, fixed lump, skin tethering, nipple retraction, nodes
Shape, margins, microcalcification, cystic or solid
Core biopsy (histology, receptors) or FNA cytology
Definitive tissue diagnosis; ER, PR, HER2 status
blocks.caption: Triple assessment

blocks.markdown:
### Oestrogen receptor and HER2 status

All invasive breast cancers are tested for **oestrogen receptor (ER)**, progesterone receptor (PR) and **human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)**. **ER-positive** tumours are driven by oestrogen: they carry a better prognosis and respond to **endocrine therapy**, for example **tamoxifen** (blocks ER in breast tissue) or **aromatase inhibitors** (block oestrogen synthesis, used in postmenopausal women). **HER2-positive** tumours have amplification of the ERBB2 gene and overexpress the HER2 receptor, which drives rapid proliferation and an aggressive course. They are treated with **trastuzumab**, a monoclonal antibody against HER2. Tumours negative for ER, PR and HER2 are called **triple negative**: they do not respond to endocrine or anti-HER2 therapy and are treated with chemotherapy and tend to be aggressive.

blocks.caption: Receptor status guides therapy (names are teaching examples, not advice)

blocks.title: Matching receptor status to treatment
blocks.prompt: Biopsy of a 58-year-old woman's lump shows invasive ductal carcinoma that is ER-positive and HER2-negative. Another patient's tumour is ER-negative and HER2-positive. Which targeted therapy suits each?

steps.text: ER-positive disease depends on oestrogen signalling, so endocrine therapy that blocks the receptor or lowers oestrogen is appropriate; in a postmenopausal woman this may be an aromatase inhibitor.
HER2-negative status means anti-HER2 therapy would not help the first patient.
The second patient's tumour will not respond to endocrine therapy because ER is absent, but overexpresses HER2 so trastuzumab is indicated, with chemotherapy.

blocks.answer: First patient: endocrine therapy; second patient: trastuzumab with chemotherapy.

blocks.markdown:
### The prostate and PSA testing

The prostate lies below the bladder, surrounding the urethra. **Benign prostatic hyperplasia** arises in the central (transition) zone and causes obstructive urinary symptoms, while most **adenocarcinomas** arise in the peripheral zone, which can be felt on digital rectal examination. **Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)** is a serine protease made by prostate epithelium that liquefies semen. It is specific to the prostate but **not specific for cancer**: levels also rise in benign enlargement, prostatitis, urinary infection, catheterisation, recent ejaculation and with age. An elevated PSA leads to prostate MRI and biopsy.

blocks.caption: Positive predictive value: the proportion of positive tests that are true positives (TP = true positives, FP = false positives).

blocks.title: How reliable is a positive PSA?
blocks.prompt: In a screening programme, 100 men have a raised PSA. Biopsy finds cancer in 30 of them. Calculate the positive predictive value and interpret it.

steps.text: Seventy per cent of men with a raised PSA do not have cancer, and many are subjected to anxiety and biopsy unnecessarily.

blocks.answer: PPV is 30%: most positive tests are false positives.

rows: Detects prostate cancer early, which may reduce prostate cancer mortality in some men (trials show a modest effect)
False positives cause anxiety and lead to biopsies
Can detect cancer in the curable stage
Overdiagnosis of slow-growing cancers that would never have caused harm
Complications of biopsy (infection, bleeding) and overtreatment (urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction)
blocks.caption: Benefits and harms of PSA testing, which is why informed, shared decision-making is advised

points: Triple assessment of a breast lump combines clinical examination, imaging (mammography and ultrasound) and core biopsy.
ER-positive cancers respond to endocrine therapy and have a better prognosis, HER2-positive cancers are aggressive but treated with trastuzumab, and triple-negative cancers need chemotherapy.
PSA is prostate-specific but not cancer-specific, so testing can find treatable cancer but also causes false positives, overdiagnosis and overtreatment.

questions.stem: Which three components make up the triple assessment of a breast lump?

options.text: Clinical assessment, imaging and tissue biopsy
Mammography, ultrasound and MRI
Tumour markers, genetic testing and imaging
History, blood tests and chest radiograph

questions.correctOptionText: Clinical assessment, imaging and tissue biopsy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: examination, imaging and pathology are the three components.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: these are all imaging modalities.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: tumour markers and genetic testing are not part of triple assessment.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: blood tests and chest radiography do not form part of it.

questions.explanation: No single method is sufficiently sensitive, so clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling are used together. Concordant benign results across all three give high confidence of a benign lesion.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has a discrete 2 cm breast lump. Which imaging modality is usually the first choice and why?

options.text: Ultrasound, because dense young breast tissue limits the sensitivity of mammography
Mammography, because it is more accurate in dense breasts
Chest radiograph, because it shows breast masses
No imaging, since lumps in young women are always benign

questions.correctOptionText: Ultrasound, because dense young breast tissue limits the sensitivity of mammography

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dense fibroglandular tissue appears white on mammography and can hide lesions, while ultrasound distinguishes cystic from solid masses.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: mammography is less sensitive in dense breasts.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a chest radiograph is not used to assess a breast lump.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: any new lump needs triple assessment.

questions.explanation: Younger breasts are denser, which lowers mammographic sensitivity. Ultrasound is therefore the primary modality, and a solid lump still requires core biopsy.

questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman has an ER-positive breast cancer. Which treatment targets the basis of this tumour's growth?

options.text: Endocrine therapy such as an aromatase inhibitor
Trastuzumab
Oestrogen supplementation
Androgen deprivation therapy

questions.correctOptionText: Endocrine therapy such as an aromatase inhibitor

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ER-positive tumours depend on oestrogen, and aromatase inhibitors reduce oestrogen synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: trastuzumab targets HER2, not ER.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: oestrogen would stimulate the tumour.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: androgen deprivation is used in prostate cancer.

questions.explanation: ER-positive cancer cells grow in response to oestrogen, so blocking the receptor or lowering oestrogen slows growth. This is why ER testing is performed on every invasive breast cancer.

questions.stem: A breast cancer shows amplification of the ERBB2 gene with strong HER2 overexpression. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It tends to be aggressive but can be treated with the anti-HER2 antibody trastuzumab
It indicates an excellent prognosis requiring no systemic treatment
It indicates responsiveness to tamoxifen alone
It excludes spread to lymph nodes

questions.correctOptionText: It tends to be aggressive but can be treated with the anti-HER2 antibody trastuzumab

distractorRationale.a: Correct: HER2 overexpression drives proliferation, but the receptor is a target for trastuzumab.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: HER2 positivity is associated with aggressive disease.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: tamoxifen acts via the ER, not HER2.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: HER2 status says nothing that excludes nodal spread.

questions.explanation: HER2 is a growth-factor receptor, and its amplification gives cells a strong proliferative drive. Because it is on the cell surface, it can be targeted by a monoclonal antibody, transforming prognosis for these tumours.

questions.stem: Which of the following can cause a raised PSA in a man without prostate cancer?

options.text: Urinary tract infection or acute prostatitis
Hypothyroidism
Anaemia
Hypertension

questions.correctOptionText: Urinary tract infection or acute prostatitis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inflammation of the prostate and urinary tract releases PSA.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: hypothyroidism does not affect PSA.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: anaemia does not affect PSA.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: hypertension does not affect PSA.

questions.explanation: PSA is specific to prostate tissue but not to cancer, and anything that disrupts the gland, such as infection, benign enlargement, catheterisation or ejaculation, can raise it. This limits its specificity as a screening test.

questions.stem: In a PSA screening study, 100 men have a raised PSA, of whom 15 are found to have cancer on biopsy and 85 do not. Calculate the positive predictive value as a percentage.
questions.explanation: PPV = TP / (TP + FP) = 15 / (15 + 85) = 0.15, or 15%. Most men with a raised PSA in this population do not have cancer, illustrating the harm of false positives.

questions.stem: Among 900 men known not to have prostate cancer, a PSA threshold is below the cut-off in 810. Calculate the specificity of the test as a percentage, using specificity = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives).
questions.explanation: True negatives are 810 and false positives are 900 - 810 = 90, so specificity is 810 / 900 = 0.90, or 90%. The remaining 10% are false positives who risk unnecessary investigation.

questions.stem: Describe the triple assessment of a breast lump and explain why imaging differs between younger and older women.
markingGuide: Clinical assessment: history, breast and axillary examination
Pathology: core needle biopsy giving histology and receptor status (FNA cytology less commonly)
Younger women have dense breasts, limiting mammography, so ultrasound is used first
Older women have more fatty breasts so mammography is effective
Concordant results give confidence; discordance needs further work-up
questions.explanation: The three components compensate for each other's limitations, and combining them is more reliable than any one alone. Imaging choice is driven by breast density.

questions.stem: Explain the significance of oestrogen receptor and HER2 status in breast cancer, including how each influences prognosis and treatment, and what is meant by triple-negative disease.
markingGuide: Endocrine therapy: tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors
HER2: ERBB2 gene amplification, receptor overexpression, aggressive proliferation
Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against HER2
Triple negative: no ER, PR or HER2, no targeted endocrine or anti-HER2 therapy, treated with chemotherapy, often aggressive
Receptor status is determined on biopsy tissue
questions.explanation: Receptor status identifies the signalling pathway on which a tumour depends and therefore the drug to which it is vulnerable. Tumours lacking all three receptors have no such target.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man asks whether he should have a PSA test. Outline the benefits and harms of PSA testing for prostate cancer, and explain why a raised PSA does not confirm cancer.
markingGuide: PSA is a prostate epithelial protease, prostate-specific but not cancer-specific
Raised in benign hyperplasia, prostatitis, infection, catheterisation, ejaculation and age
Benefit: earlier detection of potentially curable cancer, modest mortality reduction in some trials
Harm: false positives, anxiety and unnecessary biopsies
Harm: overdiagnosis of indolent cancers and overtreatment with incontinence and erectile dysfunction
False negatives and biopsy complications; shared decision-making
questions.explanation: PSA detects prostate disease of many kinds, so a positive test has low positive predictive value for clinically important cancer. Balanced counselling therefore covers both the chance of benefit and the risk of overdiagnosis.
